_: Every threshold this plugin acts on, in one place. Read it; never repeat a number from it.
_provenance: Boot budget chosen by the long-horizon A/B, 2026-09-14: 81 cells (3 budgets x 3 loads x 3 curves x 3 seeds) simulated to day 365 through the plugin's own hooks. Reproduce it with: eval/simulator/run.py --ab 20000,25000,40000 --horizon 365 --seeds 3.
_boot_budget_bytes: The @-import chain a session boots with. What the A/B established: 40,000 is ruled out (it costs ~2,762 more boot tokens every session for a boot-recall gain under the measured noise floor), and between 20,000 and 25,000 the instrument could NOT separate the arms in any load — its headline metric was DEGENERATE, reducing to 1/tokens, so it would name the smallest budget on any ballot and decides nothing by itself. The tie-break is the one piece of DOCUMENTED guidance that applies to this mechanism: Claude Code targets 'under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file', because longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. At the 101 B/line measured across real role files that is ~20,200 B, so 20,000 is the budget that guidance names.
_boot_budget_bytes_correction: This was 25,000 until 2026-09-14, justified by the auto-memory cap of 'the first 200 lines or 25 KB'. That justification was WRONG and the vault's owner caught it: that cap governs MEMORY.md only. The docs are explicit — 'This limit applies only to MEMORY.md. CLAUDE.md files are loaded in full regardless of length' (Claude Code docs, memory.md). This plugin's vault loads through @-imports from CLAUDE.md, which are never truncated, so no 25 KB cliff exists here and nothing was being bought by sitting under one. The real cost of a large boot file is context and adherence, not truncation — which is what the 200-line guidance is about, and it points at 20,000.
_boot_budget_warn_bytes: Warn on the edit that crosses this; refuse growth only past boot_budget_bytes. A door that first speaks at the moment it refuses has never given anyone a chance to act.
_boot_file_budget_bytes: The largest a region's Boot file (Kernel.md) may become before its rolling window compacts it — an 8k-token budget at the bytes/4 rule of thumb. It is a NUMBER here because in the vault this grew from it was PROSE ('budget <=8k tokens'), and prose is what three of that vault's own Boot files drifted 50-70% past while a status table printed OVER for weeks and nothing acted. A threshold a machine can read is a threshold a machine can enforce.
_boot_file_warn_bytes: Speak at this size; compact only past the budget. A door that first speaks at the moment it refuses has never given anyone a chance to act.
_compaction_floor_share: Compaction stops once the boot chain is at or below this share of the budget, rather than emptying the file. Measured against what our own boot-file graduations achieved (0.1-0.6).
_role_soft_limits_lines: Per-role line counts above which a file is offered to a cleanup pass. They are REVIEW thresholds, never delete thresholds, and a role absent from this table has no line limit. A stem here that the vault does not use costs nothing. Ethos (150) and Eidos (400) joined 2026-09-26 (DOORS-2c): the vault this grew from listed them in its own cleanup rule and the table did not, so the cleanup trigger never read the two files it named.
_boot_budget_warn_lines: The documented guidance in its own units. Kept in LINES as well as bytes because that is how the guidance is written, and because bytes-per-line varies by more than 2x across real role files (76 to 159 B/line measured) — a byte budget alone silently means a different number of lines in a terse file than in a discursive one.
_max_searchable_file_bytes: recall.py will not look inside a file larger than this, and says nothing when it skips one. The long-horizon simulation measured what that does: at medium load, day 365, 46% of held-out answers were already unreachable by tool call, and at high load 100% were -- because the rolling window pours every compacted entry into ONE growing archive file that crosses this ceiling. The number is here so a later row can read it rather than rediscover it; the fix is a SEGMENTED archive, not a larger ceiling.
_max_memory_file_bytes: The largest any memory file is allowed to become — a live role file is COMPACTED once it passes this, and an archive segment is SEALED and a new one opened before it would cross it. ONE number for both, because they are one rule: no memory file grows to where the search stops reading it. Deliberately a QUARTER of max_searchable_file_bytes — the margin is the point, not the equality, since a file allowed to sit AT the search ceiling is one oversized append from the cliff, and the failure is silent: the file simply stops being searched. Measured by the same simulation at year 3: tool recall 0.00 at high load with Aporia.md at 7,001,112 B, Canon.md 6,887,434, Errata.md 6,807,646 and Patterns.md 6,872,157 — all LIVE files, none of them archives.
_compaction_apply: Whether compaction ACTS. Off on a fresh install: the Stop hook then only records what it would move (proposals.json in the state directory) and the next session is told. Switch it on for your vault, in the `limits` object of config.json, after reading one proposal. The same holds for boot_roll_apply and worktree_sweep_apply. A chore that moves or removes your files should show you what it does before it does it.
_boot_roll_apply: Whether the Boot file's rolling window ACTS. Off until switched on per vault; see _compaction_apply.
_worktree_sweep_apply: Whether the worktree sweep REMOVES finished worktrees. Off until switched on per vault; see _compaction_apply. worktree_sweep turns the sweep off entirely; this key decides whether it acts or only reports.
_cleanup_apply: Whether the cleanup pass (cleanup.py, /gedaechtnis-cleanup) MOVES entries. Off until switched on per vault; see _compaction_apply. Until then a pass records what it would change in proposals.json and changes nothing. A run with --propose never applies, whatever this says.
_max_move_share: The largest share of one file a single automatic pass may move out of it. A file still over its limit after that is continued at the next session end. When the oldest entry alone is larger than this share, nothing is moved and the reason is reported. A quarter: a pass that removes most of a file at once is the failure this bound exists to stop.
_max_files_per_pass: The most files (or worktrees) one automatic pass may change. The rest are named and left for the next pass.
_stale_entry_days: An entry carrying a `Last revisited:` date older than this is REPORTED by the cleanup pass and never moved. Eight weeks, the interval the vault this grew from used for the same check. It is the one cleanup finding with no automatic action, deliberately: an unanswered question is not untidiness, and a pass that filed it away would hide the only thing on the list the reader actually has to do something about.
_context_hard_cap_tokens: A session at or above this much CONTEXT (input + cache_read + cache_creation at its last completed call) is told, once, that the only act it still has room for is the handoff. Absolute, not floor-relative, because the ceiling belongs to the harness and not to how much of it a session's boot spent. 700,000 is where long-running sessions actually end: measured over 30 days across 157 interactive sessions, the deepest session types peak at a median of ~500k and a p90 of 680k-790k, and the two that handed off cleanly did so at 690k and 695k. The number is a measurement of where clean endings happen, not a guess at where the limit is.
_context_warn_over_floor_tokens: How much WORK a session may add on top of its own boot floor before it is told, once, to finish the row and hand over. Floor-RELATIVE because it is a statement about work done: a session in a heavy-boot repo (measured floors run from ~80k to ~206k, median 141,965) has not done more work for having booted heavier. 400,000 puts the notice at roughly 500k-600k of total context for a typical session -- past the band where most calls happen (200k-500k) and with room left to write a handoff. The failure this prevents is not spend: it is a session that runs out of room DURING the handoff and leaves no record, which is an observed failure and not a hypothetical one.
_resume_cold_cap: A message to an IDLE session on this machine is refused when that session is COLD (its last record is older than its prompt cache lives) AND its context is at or above this many tokens; the sender is told to start the work fresh from the session's handoff. Waking a cold session writes its whole context into the cache again, while a fresh session boots from a handoff at ~100-150k. A cold session under this size is still woken. Owner ruling 2026-09-23: '300 or 350k also seem still fine ... if it's still warm and not cold after an hour. Just not loading 300k or 250k or more the next day again.' Specimen: three builders woken at 303k-494k the morning after writing their handoffs. A first line `RESUME-OVERRIDE: <reason>` sends anyway and is logged.
_resume_cold_s: The cache lifetime assumed for a session whose transcript does not say. Normally the lifetime is READ from the session's last record that created cache: 1-hour cache written means 3,600 s, otherwise 300 s, the Claude Code default of five minutes. 300 is that default, so an unknown session is judged by the shorter lifetime.
_resume_window: The context size a woken session is expected to work within (owner 2026-09-23: a warm session 'continues if it thinks it can fit the next task inside the 420-450k window'). The door prints the headroom left before this figure on every wake it lets through.
_resume_min_headroom: A wake is refused, warm or not, when the target has less than this many tokens of headroom before resume_window (i.e. at 350,000 and above by default). Owner 2026-09-23: '50k left is maybe too small'; a row does not fit in less.
_resume_short_chars: CONTEXTMSG-1: a message of at most this many characters to a WARM target passes the resume_min_headroom rule while the target is below resume_short_window. A report of a few lines costs a warm target cents and a few hundred tokens; the headroom rule exists for the next row, which such a message does not bring. The cold rules are unchanged. 0 = off (shipped): set both keys to turn it on.
_resume_short_window: CONTEXTMSG-1: the context size up to which a short message (resume_short_chars) passes the headroom rule; at or above it the headroom rule applies to every message again. 0 = off (shipped).
_split_min_entries: How many entries in one region must cluster on one sub-topic before a split is PROPOSED. Eight is the owner's own acceptance line for the sub-region row ('8 headings under one sub-topic -> one split'), not a measurement — it is the number at which a topic stops being a few related notes and starts being a room of its own. Proposing is all it does: nothing moves without an explicit name and an explicit apply.
_split_min_remaining_entries: How many entries must be LEFT IN THE PARENT for a split to be a split. Below it the cluster is still real and the proposal becomes a `refocus`, which moves NOTHING: the region keeps every entry and is offered the cluster's name as a better name for itself. Four is half the child bar, and the reasoning is symmetry — a parent left with fewer entries than half of what it takes to BE a room has stopped being the room and become the leftover. It is a number here, with this prose beside it, so that re-tuning is an edit rather than a rule change. What it guards is the n-1 case: a cluster of all-but-one entries, accepted by the old one-sided rule, leaving the parent a single orphan per role file. NOTE that it is a COUNT, so it cannot see a cluster that takes most of a large region and leaves a healthy-looking absolute number behind; whether a SHARE belongs beside it is a judgment for the vault's owner. No measurement of any particular vault is copied here — a config file carrying a frozen measurement goes stale in silence.
_split_min_remaining_share: SPLITSIM-1 experiment knob, OFF at 0.0. The SHARE of a region the parent must keep for a split to be a split, checked beside the count floor. A count floor cannot see a cluster that takes four fifths of a large region and leaves a healthy-looking absolute number; a share can. Whether it belongs on is the vault owner's call; the scenario suite under eval/scenarios/ is where the evidence is.
_split_min_cohesion: SPLITSIM-1 experiment knob, OFF at 0.0. Cohesion is measured on every cluster and reported as `cohesion` (the share of members carrying two of the cluster's three most-shared terms; a clique is 1.0). When this is set, a cluster under it is kind `diffuse`: joined pairwise by the union-find, not gathered around one subject, and `apply` refuses it. It exists because a real region's one big cluster measured 0.11-0.50 — the two-word name it would have been given was the room's two commonest words, not a topic.
_split_core_term_share: SPLITCLUSTER-1. What share of a candidate cluster's entries must carry a term for it to count as part of that cluster's CORE VOCABULARY -- and a cluster with NO core vocabulary is reported as a `chain` rather than proposed as a room. It is the difference between a subject and a chain: in a chain each entry resembles its neighbours and nothing is common to the whole, so the two-word name it would be given is the room's two commonest words rather than a topic. Measured over 10 seeds: a percolated 212-entry component scores ZERO core terms at this share on every seed, while every genuine topic measured -- cliques, and broad-vocabulary topics at three different densities -- scores at least one. ** THIS IS A THRESHOLD, NOT A CATEGORICAL TEST, and the first draft of this note wrongly claimed otherwise. ** The review that landed it built the counterexample family: blocks of entries where each block is fully joined to the next and to no other, so the commonest term is carried by 2/nblocks of the whole. Three blocks pass at 0.667, FOUR SIT EXACTLY ON 0.5 and pass only because the comparison is `>=`, five are refused. Block 1 and block 3 of the three-block case share no vocabulary at all -- a chain by this file's own definition, proposed anyway. The generated fixtures sit far on either side of the bar, which is why the separation LOOKED categorical; the honest claim is that it is measured, and that the shapes we can generate are nowhere near it. The failure mode on the wrong side is the expensive one -- a real topic refused, and until this row it was refused SILENTLY -- which is why a refusal is now reported as a chain. Lowering it admits chains; raising it starts refusing broad subjects, whose core vocabulary is small by nature.
_split_max_bridge_entries: SPLITCLUSTER-1. How many entries may be removed from a candidate cluster before it stops being ONE room. Two topics that share a few entries are welded by the pairwise rule into a single cluster named from both vocabularies; removing those few entries separates them, and they are then proposed as the two rooms they are. Measured over 6 seeds: a fused pair comes apart at exactly the number of entries bridging it (1, 2, 3, 4), while five genuine single topics do not come apart at ANY cut up to 6 -- so this number is bounded by the COST of the search, not by the risk of cutting a real topic in half. That measurement was taken BEFORE the density shortcut existed, by running every search to exhaustion; the shortcut now refuses those same searches up front on the dense ones. Same conclusion, different route -- worth knowing if the figure is ever re-derived. RAISE it to see fuses held by more entries, at C(16, K) connectivity passes per cluster ON A SPARSE ONE -- a dense cluster is skipped before the search starts (a cut of size K implies some entry has degree at most (n-K)/2 - 1 + K, so a better-connected least-connected entry proves no such cut exists), which is why a 1000-entry clique costs 0.4s rather than 60. The shapes where the search does real work, sparse and bridged, are unchanged at roughly 6-7s per 1000 entries. What it CANNOT see, said plainly: a pair bridged by more than this many entries is still reported as one topic.
_split_boilerplate_region_share: SPLITVOCAB-1. The VAULT-WIDE axis, beside the region-relative one: what share of the vault's VOTING regions must write a term -- twice or more in that region, so not in passing -- before it is treated as HOUSE STYLE and removed from the vocabulary the split rule clusters and names on. It exists because a dry run over the author's own vault would have created five rooms and named four of them from document conventions (ScopeLocked, ScopeCanonical, NotesNever, FixedImages): `scope` is carried by 23.7% of all 1,133 entries there, and the region-relative core-vocabulary test cannot see any of it, because boilerplate passes that test BY BEING EVERYWHERE. ** WHY BREADTH AND NOT FREQUENCY: ** vault-wide frequency does not separate -- sorted it runs 23.7, 16.9, 10.6, ... 4.1, 3.9, 3.4 with the first genuine topic word sitting among furniture words -- so any frequency bar is a number chosen to fit the four names that went wrong. Breadth does better: the term that WELDED each wrong name is written in 8 or more regions (scope 13, never 13, notes 11, fixed 8) and every topical term in that sample in 6 or fewer -- though not every word in those names is, since `locked`, `canonical` and `images` came along as the second word at breadth 5, 5 and 1. ** THAT IS NOT A GAP IN THE DISTRIBUTION, ** which is a continuum (17 terms at breadth 8, 13 at 7, 40 at 6), and the band sitting exactly on the bar holds `split`, `region`, `owner`, `layer`, `surface` -- one region's real subjects. EVERY setting of this strips some subject words; what was measured is which ROOMS come out. ** WHY 0.41: ** running the whole vault at every bar gives, with the axis OFF, 5 rooms of which four are named from conventions -- the defect -- then 5 differently-named rooms at bar 4, 1 room at bars 5-7, ZERO rooms at bar 8 -- the rule silent over 1,134 entries -- and 3 rooms at bar 9, two named from conventions again. A share turns the vault's SIZE into the bar and a vault gains a region whenever a repo is onboarded, so the number is set for OUTCOME STABILITY: 0.41 puts the bar at 7 today and puts today's 15 voters in the middle of the 13-to-17 range over which the bar stays 6 or 7. At 0.45 the bar was also 7 and ONE more voting region would have made it 8, which is the silent failure. ** WHY VOTERS AND NOT REGIONS: ** a region counts toward the denominator only if it writes SOME term twice. Eleven of this vault's twenty-eight regions were an incident snapshot copied in, 0-3 entries each, carrying no term twice and destined for the Trash; they changed no breadth count and they would have set the bar, re-calibrating the axis the day the folder was tidied. Measured both ways: 28 regions and 17, 15 voters either way. The vote SATURATES at two entries, so a stub counts as much as a 266-entry region -- the stable band above is the protection against that, and it is a band, not a proof. ** WHAT IT CANNOT DO: ** it needs at least three VOTING regions (a floor in split.py, not a knob), so on the one-region-per-repository vault this package creates by default the axis finds NOTHING; and up to seven voters that floor sets the bar rather than this share. Set to 0 to switch the axis off entirely; lower it to strip more words, at the cost of silencing real topics written in house style -- which fails SILENTLY, since a room that is never proposed is never seen.
_split_auto_apply: SPLITAUTO-1. Whether the plugin may create a sub-region ITSELF, with nobody in the loop for the MOVE. The owner's bar, in his words, is that a non-expert should never be asked to move a file -- 'human moves' was the interim, not the target -- and his condition for this shipping ON was ZERO false splits in the scenario suite. It is `split_auto_min_remaining_share` that earns that ON THE SUITE, so read its note before changing either. ** IT SHIPS OFF ANYWAY, on a measurement rather than on caution: ** a dry run over the author's own 1,133-entry vault would have created five rooms and named four of them after DOCUMENT CONVENTIONS instead of subjects -- ScopeLocked, ScopeCanonical, NotesNever -- because `scope` occurs in 23.7% of every entry in that vault (the Scope: line each Canon entry carries) and `never` in 16.9%. The core-vocabulary rule cannot catch that: boilerplate is carried by far MORE than half a room, so it passes by being everywhere. SPLITVOCAB-1 has since landed and this still ships OFF, on the re-measurement rather than on caution: with the vault-wide boilerplate axis in place the same vault's five rooms become ONE -- 9 of one 101-entry region's entries under a name built from that region's own subject, parent keeping 91% -- and that room gathers a shipping note, a sync bug and a pattern about blind review, at cohesion 0.556. The owner's condition for ON was ZERO false auto-applies on the live vault, and one arguable room is not zero. Set true and `--auto` will create rooms; `--auto --dry-run` reports what would move either way, and is how you check whether the names read like topics in YOUR vault before trusting it with the move.
_split_auto_min_remaining_share: How much of a region the parent must KEEP for the plugin to move the rest by itself. A proposal that takes most of a region out is not a split; it is the parent being renamed through the back door, and that is a decision the reader wants. ** COHESION CANNOT EXPRESS THIS AND IS ANTI-CORRELATED WITH IT: ** measured over 10 seeds, the two cases the reader does NOT want moved (S07, 212 of 266; S13, 34 of 40) both score cohesion 1.000, the MAXIMUM, while a genuine broad topic that should move scores 0.45-0.60 -- so a cohesion bar high enough to hold those two holds everything. The moved SHARE does express it, and this bar sits in a measured gap: parent keeps 15% (S13) HOLD, 20% (S07) HOLD, 20% (S21) held too and that is a MISS rather than an error, then 33% (S04/S05) move, and 47-83% for every proposal on the real vault. ** THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES IT SAFE: ** holding a genuine split back costs nothing, because it is still PROPOSED and the reader still sees it; moving wrongly costs a restructured vault. So the bar holds everything the reader wants held and knowingly holds S21 with it.
_lesson_push_enabled:
LESSONPUSH-1 and LESSONPUSH-2. Whether the plugin surfaces lessons this vault already holds after a write. ** IT SHIPS OFF, AND TWO DESIGNS' GATES ARE WHY. THE SECOND REFUSAL CLOSES PUSH-AT-WRITE-TIME. ** The idea is sound and the measurement refused it twice, on different matchers and different triggers.

DESIGN 1 (term overlap between the write and a lesson HEADING, PostToolUse on Edit/Write, `ec716757`): (1) NO SEPARATION -- the top score of an edit against its own region's lessons had a median of 0.358-0.369 across four seeds, and the same corpus scored against a DIFFERENT region's edit text -- same idf, same mass reference, same number of draws -- had a median of 0.352-0.371, with a p95 up to 0.610 against the real signal's p75 of 0.427. The noise median sat ON the signal median, so no bar existed that fired and was above its own floor. (2) NO HELD-OUT HIT -- of the 17 lessons LESSONYIELD-1 measured as RE-OCCURRING, 6 were checkable and 0 were surfaced at any threshold including zero. (3) A BLIND TRIGGER -- Edit/Write/MultiEdit is 543 of 3,294 file-producing tool calls in that population, 16.9%, because five writes in six here go through a Bash heredoc or redirect.

DESIGN 2 (this one: a CITATION matcher -- a lesson is surfaced when the write touches a path, queue-row id, ruling id, backticked name or wikilinked heading that the lesson's OWN BODY cites -- plus a second trigger on Bash commands that literally produce a file). The trigger was fixed and the matcher was not: (1) TRIGGER COVERAGE ROSE 16.5% -> 50.0% of file-producing tool calls (543 Edit/Write + 1,105 Bash with a literal target, of 3,294), and in a 200-call audit of real Bash commands the detector claimed a target in 17 and every one was a real write. (2) STILL NO SEPARATION -- a citation match is exact, so the floor is the index's FALSE-POSITIVE RATE: real writes fire on 44-47% of a 400-write sample, and the SAME index against a foreign write's tokens fires on 50-66%. The separation ratio is 0.708 at the recorded seed and 0.67-0.90 over four seeds -- BELOW ONE, meaning the index fires slightly MORE on a write it has nothing to do with. Re-measured with the tautology rule disabled on both arms, to remove the one asymmetry in the control, the reading is the same (0.71-0.83). (3) STILL NO HELD-OUT HIT -- with Bash writes visible, 8 of the 17 rows became checkable (up from 6) and 0 were surfaced; in every one of the 8 the lesson cited NOTHING the write touched, so it never entered the ranking at all. That is a statement about the SEAM, not about the tuning. (4) The cost also rose: 13.1% of writes fire, a median session sees 5 lines, against design 1's 1.8% and 0.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY. It does not say lessons are useless -- LESSONYIELD-1 measured hook-ENFORCED lessons re-occurring at about half the rate of kernel-PUSHED ones. It says the WRITE MOMENT is not where a lesson can be found: at write time all that is known is the text and the path, and neither the words nor the citations in them reach the lesson that was about to be re-broken. The next candidate named by the row and NOT built is a BOOT-TIME arm, where the session's whole subject is known before any work happens. Everything in the two modules below describes what they do if a vault sets this key true anyway.
_lesson_push_max_per_fire: LESSONPUSH-1. How many lesson lines one edit may produce. Two, because the notice is a NOTE appended to a PostToolUse the session did not ask for: the cost of a wrong line is paid on every call and the benefit of a right one is paid once. Not measured -- there is no experiment here that could separate two from three, and saying so is better than dressing a judgment as a finding.
_lesson_push_max_per_session: LESSONPUSH-1. The whole session's budget, after which the arm is silent and -- because the cap is checked before any file is read -- costs nothing at all. Ten is the point at which a repeated note stops being read, the same reasoning `context_cap` uses for firing once per level. Measured at the shipped threshold the cap is never reached (median 0 lines per session, max 5); at a permissive 0.0 it binds hard (median 10), which is what a cap is for.
_agent_max_concurrent: AGENTFANOUT-1. The most sub-agents one session may have alive at once: WARN on the call that reaches it, DENY above it. MEASURED, not chosen: `scripts/agent_concurrency.py` reads every sub-agent transcript on this machine (`<projects>/<project>/<parent-session-id>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl`), takes each transcript's first and last record as the interval it was alive, and computes the maximum number of OVERLAPPING intervals inside each parent session. Over the 30 days to 2026-09-20 the population was 99 sessions that ran at least one sub-agent (2,306 sub-agents, 0 transcripts unreadable): peak concurrency median 3, p90 8, p95 11, max 24. Eight is the p90 by nearest rank, so it is a number sessions here actually reach, and the two tails it cuts are the ones this key exists for: the 24-peak session is the 2026-09-20 fan-out that burned 30% of a five-hour window in about five minutes. A session that genuinely needs more raises it in the vault's config `limits` object, which is a recorded act.
_agent_open_stale_seconds: AGENTFANOUT-1. How long an unclosed sub-agent slot counts against the cap. There is no SubagentStart event, so the live count is kept by the plugin: the gate adds a slot when it allows an `Agent` call and `subagent_stop.py` removes one when a sub-agent ends. A sub-agent whose Stop never fires — a crash, a killed session, a harness that stops sending the event — would otherwise hold its slot forever and the door would close a little further on every delegation until it refused everything. Six hours is longer than any sub-agent measured here (the longest observed interval in the 30-day population is under two hours) and short enough that a wedged count clears within one working session. It is a SAFETY VALVE, not a threshold anyone should tune to bite.
_lesson_push_boot_enabled:
LESSONPUSH-3, the BOOT arm -- the THIRD and LAST design of the lesson push, and the one the row that ordered it said would END the push line either way. ** IT SHIPS OFF, ON ITS OWN GATES, AND THAT CLOSES THE PUSH LINE: three designs, three measured refusals. ** 

WHY A THIRD DESIGN EXISTED AT ALL. Designs 1 and 2 failed at the same seam and it was not the matcher: term overlap and citation resolution are unrelated matchers over the same TRIGGER POINT, and both returned zero on the same held-out set, because at write time the system knows a path and a blob of text and the lesson about to be re-broken is reachable from neither. At BOOT the session's subject is known before any work happens. So this arm matches no edit: it selects lesson entries whose citations appear in the session's STRUCTURAL SURFACE -- its resolved @-import chain, the OPEN rows of its own work queues, and (on a resume, where the transcript already exists) its opening prompt.

WHAT THE GATES SAID, over the same population the two write arms were measured on (92 transcripts, 2026-08-01..2026-09-20, the LESSONYIELD-1 census corpus):

(1) NOISE FLOOR -- THE ONLY GATE OF THE THREE DESIGNS THAT ANY ARM HAS EVER PASSED. A selector with no score has no threshold, so the floor is a matched CONTROL, and a boot selection has two inputs so there are two: swap the lesson CORPUS to a foreign region and hold the surface fixed -- median set overlap 0.25; swap the SURFACE to another lane's repo chain and queue rows and hold the corpus fixed -- median overlap 0.11. ZERO identical sets in 40 sampled sessions. Over FIFTEEN seeds the corpus control is 0.25 every time and the surface control is 0.11 in twelve and 0.25 in three -- a range of 0.11 to 0.25, never above the corpus control and never near one. (The first four seeds agreed to four decimal places, and the row's reviewer was right that a wider sweep does not: the pool of foreign lanes on one machine is small, so the surface figure is modal rather than fixed. The gate's reading is unchanged at either value.) Design 2's equivalent separation ratio was BELOW ONE. The selector is genuinely reading both of its inputs.

(2) HELD-OUT -- 1 HIT OF 17, against a bar of 3, and the bar was set before the run. Of the 17 re-occurrence rows: 9 UNCHECKED (8 because the census note names no artifact file to join a session on, 1 because the lesson was not in the vault under that heading on the day), and of the 8 checkable, ONE would have been in the session's five-line block (at rank 4), one was selected at rank 6 -- just outside -- two were live candidates the session was not pointed at, and FOUR cite nothing at all and are therefore unreachable by any citation-based arm, which is design 2's recorded blindness arriving unchanged. Each session's block was reconstructed AS OF THAT DAY: the lesson corpus and the queue rows are materialised from the vault's git history at the row's own date, because both grow weekly and today's versions contain rows the work itself created. The repo-side `CLAUDE.md` is today's, which flatters the arm.

(3) RELEVANCE -- a reviewer judged 40 boot BLOCKS; the figure is in the row report. It could not change the verdict: the row's rule is >=60% relevant AND >=3 held-out hits, and gate 2 is 1.

** THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE VERDICT: THE ARM HAS LANE RESOLUTION, NOT SESSION RESOLUTION. ** Over 92 sessions the block was IDENTICAL in all 92 -- one distinct block, five lines, 747 bytes, ~187 tokens, 0.13% of the measured median boot floor of 141,965. That is not a tuning fault: the boot chain and the open queue rows are properties of the LANE AND THE DAY, not of the session, and they are the only two inputs a cold start has. Given the opener as well -- a diagnostic arm, `--boot-with-opener` -- 20 of 40 sampled blocks become distinct and the held-out result does NOT move (still 1 of 17). ** AND THE OPENER IS NOT AVAILABLE AT A COLD START: ** measured on the author's machine, the first user record was written AFTER the SessionStart hook in 96 of 97 sessions, median +0.86 s. So a per-session boot push is only reachable on a RESUME, and even there it did not reach the held-out set.

WHAT THIS CLOSES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It closes PUSH: three designs, two triggers, three matchers, refused by their own gates. It does not say lessons are useless -- LESSONYIELD-1 measured hook-ENFORCED lessons re-occurring at about half the rate of kernel-PUSHED ones, and that is the direction SYSTEMYIELD-1 now has to test: enforcement against prose. Set this true and every session in a lane will get the same five lines; the module, the replay arm (`eval/lesson_push_replay.py --boot`) and both control arms stay in the tree as the record.
_lesson_push_boot_max_lines: LESSONPUSH-3. How many lesson lines the boot block may carry. Five, from the row that ordered the arm, and NOT tuned afterwards: one of the two held-out lessons the selector reached landed at rank 6, and raising the cap to six would have bought a second hit and a third of a bar -- which is tuning past a refusal, the thing this arc's own rule forbids. Measured at five the block is 747 bytes, about 187 tokens, 0.13% of the median boot floor. The cost is paid by EVERY session rather than by every write, which is why this arm's bar was set higher than the write arms' and why the figure is reported against the floor rather than on its own. Zero switches the arm off the same way `lesson_push_boot_enabled` does.
_lazy_bodies_enabled: LAZYBOOT-1 item 2. When true, the first time a session touches a path under a GRADUATED region (one carrying a Boot file), that region's pull-only bodies are injected once as PostToolUse additionalContext -- Cursor's Auto Attached mechanism, keyed on path prefix and never on content. Ships FALSE, for a reason that is measured rather than cautious: the saving this arm belongs to was already banked by items 1 and 3 (Boot files placed, the repos' CLAUDE.md swapped to import them), and this arm ADDS cost -- it charges a session that works in a region roughly what that region's bodies weigh, on top of a boot that no longer carries them. It is worth switching on for a lane that works in one region all day and wrong for a session that touches six. The three arms before it were all refused by their own gates after shipping-by-default was assumed; this one records the measurement and leaves the switch to the vault that installs it.
_lazy_body_max_bytes: The most one region's bodies may inject in a single fire. 60,000 B is ~15,000 tokens at the bytes/4 rule of thumb -- roughly three times a graduated region's Boot-file budget (32,000 B would buy less than the thing it replaces) and under the body set of every graduated region measured on the vault this was built against. ** THE CAP BITES ON ALMOST THE WHOLE POPULATION, and that is stated here because the first draft of this note did not say so.** Measured over the 9 graduated regions of that vault (the population; `lazy_body.bodies_for` is the instrument): 8 of 9 exceed 60,000 B, from 89,436 B to 842,859 B, and the 9th is within 7,232 B of it. So a PARTIAL injection with the skipped files named is the NORM for this arm, not an edge case -- the full-record case is the exception. The degrade path is correct and has its own controls, but a reader choosing this number should know they are choosing how much of a record to truncate, not whether truncation happens. Bodies are offered in BODY_ORDER (Status, Decisions, Mistakes, Rules first), so what the cap cuts is the descriptive tail, never the record a session is about to contradict. Zero switches the arm off the same way `lazy_bodies_enabled` does.
_facets_enabled: KERNELFACET-1. A facet is a rule file beside a region's Boot file, named Kernel-<name>.md, whose frontmatter names what loads it: tool-name globs (tools), regexes searched in a Bash command (bash), path globs (paths), q-id globs (rows); a prompt carrying facet:<name> also loads it. The first matching tool call or prompt injects the facet once for the session, as additionalContext, and writes one row to facets.log (session id, facet, trigger, bytes). Ships TRUE because a region with no facet file costs nothing: nothing is injected and one 'none' log row per session records that there was nothing to fire. The trigger lives in the facet file, never in this package.
_facet_max_bytes: KERNELFACET-1. The largest facet body injected whole. A facet over this size is NAMED instead (path and size) so the session reads it directly; the point of a facet is to be smaller than the Boot file it came out of. 24,000 B is about 6,000 tokens at bytes/4. Zero means no cap.
_worktree_sweep: WTSWEEP-1. Whether the Stop hook removes GIT worktrees that are finished — HEAD an ancestor of main AND a clean status AND no live session working in them — and records the rest for the next SessionStart to report. This is `git worktree`, NOT the APFS clones in worktree.py, which this never touches. Ships TRUE: the arc it comes from left 45 abandoned worktree folders because removing one was a thing every builder had to remember. Set false to make the sweep report-only.
_triggers: OR semantics: any one arm firing is enough. Ported from the vault Stop hook's sections 3 and 5 by row R1, which reads them from here and holds no copy.
_kernel_entry_door: The kernel-entry door (hooks/kernelentry.py, KERNELENTRY-1): an ADDED bullet in a region's Kernel.md that carries a tool signature (a command, `claude -p`, a .html path, a path glob, a script path, a tool name, shell syntax) is pointed at the facet whose trigger matches it. Only a signature NEW to the file fires (KERNELENTRY-2): one no bullet of the file before the write already carries, so rewording a bullet, adding a facet name to a list or moving a command between bullets passes, while a command that stood only in prose or a fenced block and is now put into a bullet counts as new. On by default because it only WARNS until a DENY date is set below: a note in the model's next turn, never a refusal.
_kernel_entry_deny_from: The day (YYYY-MM-DD) the kernel-entry door starts REFUSING. Empty = WARN forever. The flip is a date in the config so it does not depend on anyone remembering it (the partition door's hand flip stayed undone for eight days); the vault's owner sets it, 14 days after the door goes live, in the `limits` object of config.json.
_apostrophe_door: The apostrophe-regime door (hooks/apostrophe_door.py, APOSTROPHEGATE-1): in a repo whose owner declared its layers in `.gedaechtnis-apostrophe`, a write that adds an in-word apostrophe (a Cyrillic letter on both sides) in a codepoint other than its layer's (U+02BC or U+0027) is named. Silent in every repo without that file. On by default because it only WARNS until a DENY date is set below.
_apostrophe_deny_from: The day (YYYY-MM-DD) the apostrophe door starts REFUSING such a write. Empty = WARN forever.
_rule_doors: DOORS-2 (hooks/ruledoors.py): six rules a script can decide, each a door that WARNS until its `<door>_deny_from` date and REFUSES from that day on, inside the vault or a repo carrying an `.atlas-lane` marker (a note elsewhere). secret: an API key, token, private key or card number added to any file but a `.env`. html_head: a whole HTML page whose first two lines are not `<!doctype html>` and `<meta charset="utf-8">`, or whose meta ends past byte 1024. launch_pin: a `claude` launch without `--model` and `--effort`. judge_md: a new Markdown file that asks its reader for a verdict (a verdict/judge name or heading and two or more unmarked choices). row_identity: an added queue row whose backticked `q:` anchor and `| q:` field disagree. marker_roster: an `.atlas-lane` marker whose `path:` lines differ from its lane's roster row, or the other way round — WARN ONLY, with no deny date, because the two-places change is two writes and refusing the first would make the rule impossible to follow. `<door>_door: false` turns one off. Every judgment is a line in ruledoors.log. The dates are the vault owner's to set, like kernel_entry_deny_from.
_kill_door: The kill door (hooks/killdoor.py, KILLDOOR-1): a Bash `kill`, `pkill` or `killall` whose target comes from a command substitution, backticks, a variable or `xargs`; `pkill -P`, `pkill -f` and `pgrep -f` always; pid 0, pid 1 and negative pids. `kill <digits>` typed out passes, and `kill -0` with any target (signal 0 sends nothing). Specimen 2026-09-28: `pkill -P $(pgrep -o -f x || echo 1)` became `pkill -P 1` and ended every app on the machine. WARNS until `kill_deny_from`, then REFUSES inside the vault or a marked repo (a note elsewhere), like the DOORS-2 doors.
_kill_deny_from: The day (YYYY-MM-DD) the kill door starts REFUSING. Empty = WARN forever. The vault owner's to set.
_facts_max_bytes: The SessionStart facts block's cap, in bytes, operating rules included (hooks/factsbudget.py, BOOTFACTS-1). Over it, whole tiers of long-tail lines move behind /gedaechtnis-status in a fixed order: memory-file lists, other regions' Boot-file alarms, the worktree list, state-file pointers. 0 = no cap, so a stranger's install is unchanged until it opts in. Measured 2026-09-26 over the 20 newest real sessions: 10,922-12,140 B, median 11,531 B, every one past facts_inline_limit_chars, so the model read a 2 KB preview. Proposal for a vault: 8000 (20% under the inline limit, room for the operating rules' ~4,800 B).
_facts_inline_limit_chars: Past this many characters the harness does not inline a hook's output: it saves it to a file and shows the model a 2 KB preview. Measured, not documented: over the newest ~400 sessions the largest facts block shown whole was 9,835 chars and the smallest one cut to a preview 10,127. A block past it gets a warning line second in the block, where the preview still shows it.
_context_reach_margin_tokens: TERMOVERLOAD-1: how many tokens BEFORE the resume gate's refusal bound (resume_window - resume_min_headroom) the REACH notice fires, so a session can bring its handoff up to date while it can still be messaged. 0 fires at the bound itself.
_session_cap: TERMOVERLOAD-1, SESSCLOSE-2: WORKING claude sessions on this machine (registry status not idle; a session with no record counts as working) at or above which `sessions.py launch` refuses a new session, with the count and the idle sessions named. 0 = no cap (the count is still printed). The number is the owner's (specimen 2026-09-26: 84 processes, load 90, a builder's suite killed).
_session_close_apply: TERMOVERLOAD-1: whether the session-close sweep CLOSES (kill -9 of the pid recorded at launch) a session it finds finished, or only proposes. Off until the owner switches it on; see _compaction_apply.
_session_close_idle_minutes: TERMOVERLOAD-1, SESSCLOSE-2: how long a FINISHED session's last turn must have ENDED (an assistant end_turn, nothing pending, no background task open) before the close sweep proposes it. Never a reason on its own: every other close rule must hold too. 180 since SESSCLOSE-2: the replay of 2026-09-24..27 found finished sessions re-used by their orchestrator up to 139 minutes after their handoff; 150 and 180 both replayed with zero would-be wrong closes, 120 with two.
_session_close_exempt: SESSCLOSE-2: session names (shell-style patterns, e.g. "mnemosyne-*") the close sweep never proposes or closes, whatever their state. Empty by default; the owner's list.
_session_cap_per_seat: SESSCLOSE-2: working sessions one orchestrator (the seat whose shell runs `sessions.py launch`, or --seat) may have live at once; a launch over it is refused. 0 = off. The number is the owner's.
_session_close_every_s: TERMOVERLOAD-1: the machine-wide minimum interval between two close-sweep passes. The sweep runs on Stop, which fires in every session; one pass per interval is enough.
_session_launch_door: TERMOVERLOAD-1: what the Bash door does with a command that starts a claude session outside `sessions.py launch` (a Terminal window, or screen/tmux without the environment scrub): off | warn | deny. deny is the owner's.
_session_swap_cap_share: TERMOVERLOAD-1, SESSCLOSE-2: swap in use, as a share of swap total (0-1) — or, on a machine with no swap (total 0), memory in use by the memory-pressure reading (macOS kern.memorystatus_level) — at or above which `sessions.py launch` refuses a new session. 0 = off. The number is the owner's (the seat's measure 2026-09-26: 16 sessions, load 51, swap 2.4 of 4 GB = 0.60 — memory, not the process count, was the line).
